The energy crisis of 2021–2023 had widespread effects

. Firms and households experienced direct increases in energy costs and faced higher input costs stemming from rising energy prices. This led to significant price increases across goods and services. However, this occurred alongside supply chain disruptions caused by lockdowns, as well as fiscal stimulus and accommodative monetary policy aimed at supporting economies and individuals during the COVID-19 crisis, all of which contributed to rising inflation (Barrett, 2022). Neufeld (2022) reports that inflation surpassed target levels in all advanced economies and in 87% of emerging economies in 2022, as opposed to 9% and 20%, respectively, in 2019. Rampant inflation eroded consumer purchasing power and confidence, denting expenditure. To fight inflation, central banks increased interest rates to levels not seen since the 2008 Global Financial Crisis (GFC), raising the cost of borrowing, reducing investment, and hindering economic growth. Energy price shocks and inflation are considered significant factors hindering the post-COVID-19 economic recovery (Neufeld, 2022). Governments worldwide introduced various schemes such as price caps and energy support payments to shield consumers from high energy prices or, at the very least, reduce concerns about rising energy prices (Sgaravatti, Tagliapietra, & Zachmann, 2023).

(van Hoof & Vishnoi, 2022). Research on the energy crisis has primarily focused on its macroeconomic effects, confirming the adverse consequences on household expenditure and production (Guan et al., 2023; Hutter & Weber, 2022).

Focusing exclusively on one aspect of the energy crisis, the Russia-Ukraine war, studies by Alam, Tabash, Billah, Kumar, and Anagreh (2022), Umar, Polat, Choi, and Teplova (2022) and Adekoya, Asl, Oliyide, and Izadi (2023), among others, find a more intensive impact of oil prices on stock markets in the period immediately following Russia's invasion. Studies such as those of Maghyereh, Awartani, and Bouri (2016), Dutta, Noor, and Dutta (2017) and Bouri, Lien, Roubaud, and Shahzad (2018) report that oil price uncertainty, measured by the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) Crude Oil Volatility Index (OVX), reduces stock returns and triggers volatility (see Section 2 for more details). However, research investigating the effects of broader energy price uncertainty on stock markets is limited. To the best of our knowledge, the one exception to this is the study of Chiah, Phan, Tran, and Zhong (2022) who, using a low frequency (monthly) measure of energy price uncertainty, find that energy price uncertainty increases the value premium. Despite these insights, gaps remain. Notably, there is an absence of a high-frequency (daily) measure of energy price uncertainty. Furthermore, there is limited understanding of how energy price uncertainty evolved throughout the global energy crisis. This is especially pertinent given the multitude of triggers, and how stock markets responded to this evolving form of uncertainty. In this study, we investigate the evolution and impact of uncertainty stemming from the global energy crisis on global markets, represented by the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI). We designate the start of the global energy crisis as 1 June 2021, following observed rapid increases in energy prices which are most notable for natural gas and coal. We use wavelet coherence to study the evolving relationship between energy price uncertainty (ENPU) and overall uncertainty and apply least squares regressions and ARCH/GARCH modelling to quantify ENPU's impact on global market returns and volatility. Our study contributes to the literature in several areas. First, we develop a broad daily measure of energy price uncertainty, ENPU, that encompasses oil, natural gas, and coal price uncertainty and, which we argue and show, is better suited to capturing the nature of the global energy crisis. The ENPU index uses Google searches to isolate and quantify energy price uncertainty experienced by stock markets by applying a two-step approach that combines multipath General-to-Specific (GETS) modelling and elastic net regression (Hoover & Perez, 1999; Sucarrat & Escribano, 2012). Where our study differs from others that utilise Google searches to model uncertainty, is that our approach directly isolates and approximates components of overall stock market uncertainty, as measured by the CBOE's Volatility Index (VIX) (Szczygielski, Charteris, Bwanya, & Brzeszczyński, 2024; Szczygielski, Charteris, Obojska, & Brzeszczyński, 2024). While measures of energy price uncertainty exist, these suffer from limitations. Studies that use daily measures consider a single component of energy price uncertainty, namely oil (Bouri et al., 2018; Dutta et al., 2017; Xiao, Hu, Ouyang, & Wen, 2019). Yet, the present crisis is characterised by record-high natural gas and coal prices. Other studies utilise conditional variance estimates of changes in the real monthly United States (U.S.) Fuel and Related Products and Power series to capture energy price uncertainty (see Chiah et al., 2022; Yoon & Ratti, 2011). Our study, which investigates energy price uncertainty, differs from studies that focus on energy uncertainty which refers to the ambiguity surrounding the future of energy markets, encompassing fluctuations in energy prices, supply and demand imbalance and broader factors such as geopolitical tensions, regulatory changes and macroeconomic conditions. An example of a study that focuses on energy uncertainty is that of Xu, Fu, and Lau (2021), who propose a broad energy market uncertainty index incorporating energy prices, demand, supply, inventories and key macroeconomic and financial variables. Another is that of Dang, Nguyen, Lee, Nguyen, and Le (2023) who use textual analysis to construct an energy uncertainty index. They employ an extensive set of search terms related to energy prices, regulation, environmental impact, renewable energy, electric vehicles and crises. However, the measures of Xu et al., 2021 and Dang et al. (2023) are only available monthly and do not focus on energy price uncertainty exclusively. Additionally, neither of these studies investigate the impact of energy uncertainty on stock markets, instead examining the impact on oil prices and economic output, respectively. Second, we show that the ENPU index encompasses most of the information reflected in, and is more comprehensive than, the OVX, a commonly used proxy for energy price uncertainty. Examples of studies that use the OVX as a measure of energy price uncertainty and apply it to model its impact on stock returns and volatility are those of Maghyereh, Awartani, and Bouri (2016), Xiao, Zhou, Wen, and Wen (2018), Choi and Hong (2020) and Lin and Su (2020), amongst others (see Section 2 for a more extensive discussion). Zhao et al. (2023) state that researchers have focused their attention mainly on oil price movements when studying the effect of energy price volatility on economic growth, attributing this to the extensive use of oil and suggesting that the influence of other energy prices is often ignored. However, the present crisis differs in character from previous energy crises. For example, oil prices experienced peaks (of over $120/barrel), similar to those during the energy crisis of 2011 and 2012, and rapid declines between mid-2014 and 2016 (from over $110/barrel to close to $20/barrel). Extreme oil price movements are therefore not novel. In contrast, coal and natural gas prices have remained relatively stable in recent history, potentially explaining why energy price uncertainty has been measured using the OVX.

Peaks in coal and natural gas prices observed during the global energy crisis can be viewed as unusual occurrences in recent times (see Fig. 1). Given that this crisis is different from previous ones, this calls for an energy price uncertainty measure that also reflects uncertainty around coal and natural gas prices as well as oil prices. This is particularly pertinent given that uncertainty is one of the transmission channels through which energy prices impact financial markets (Brown & Yücel, 2002). Several studies examine how the Russia-Ukraine war has influenced the relationship between energy prices and stock markets over the short run. Adekoya, Asl, Oliyide, and Izadi (2023) find oil prices had a greater impact on the stock markets of ten developed countries during the war's initial phase (24 February to 31 March 2022) than before the war.
